title: TSMC says 'A16' chipmaking tech to arrive in 2026, setting up showdown with Intel - ET Telecom
text:
- Devices
- 2 min read
TSMC says 'A16' chipmaking tech to arrive in 2026, setting up showdown with Intel
Kevin Zhang, TSMC's senior vice president of business development, told reporters that the company has developed its new A16 chipmaking process faster than expected because of demand from AI chip firms, without naming specific customers.
By Stephen Nellis
SANTA CLARA: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co said on Wednesday that a new chip manufacturing technology called "A16" will enter production in the second half of 2026, setting up a showdown with longtime rival Intel over who can make the world's fastest chips.
TSMC, the world's biggest contract manufacturer of advanced computing chips and a key supplier to Nvidia and Apple, announced the news at a conference in Santa Clara, California, where TSMC executives said that makers of AI chips will likely be the first adopters of the technology rather than a smartphone maker.
Analysts told Reuters that the technologies announced on Wednesday could call into question Intel's claims in February that it will overtake TSMC in making the world's fastest computing chips with a new technology Intel calls "14A."
Kevin Zhang, TSMC's senior vice president of business development, told reporters that the company has developed its new A16 chipmaking process faster than expected because of demand from AI chip firms, without naming specific customers.
AI chip firms "really want to optimize their designs to get every ounce of performance we have," Zhang said.
Zhang said that TSMC does not believe it needs to use a ASML's new "High NA EUV" lithography tool machines to build the A16 chips. Intel last week revealed that it plans to be the first to use the machines, which can cost $373 million each, to develop its 14A chip.
TSMC also revealed a new technology for suppling power to computer chips from the backside of the chip, which helps speed up AI chips and will be available in 2026.

title: Spotting AI Washing: How Companies Overhype Artificial Intelligence
text:
Although I firmly believe AI is a hugely transformative technology that will change the world in many ways, it’s also clear that there is a lot of hype and hot air around the subject!
It’s something that inevitably occurs with any exciting technology, particularly when there’s a lot of money to be made.
This is no surprise, given that past studies have shown that startups that mention ‘AI’ attract 15 percent to 50 percent more investment than those that don’t!
So, it’s important to be able to tell the difference between what’s real and what is being concocted by marketing departments simply interested in what they can sell us.
Here, I'll be looking at the phenomenon of AI washing – what it is, who is doing it, why it is dangerous, and perhaps most importantly, how to spot it.
What Is AI Washing?
In basic terms, AI washing involves exaggerating the capabilities of a product or service that is sold as ‘AI’ in order to make it look more sophisticated, innovative or intelligent than it actually is.
It can be seen as a form of bandwagon jumping. The term itself derives from ‘greenwashing’, which is frequently used to describe projects, products or services that overstate how environmentally-friendly they are, to appeal to eco-conscious consumers.
Marketers attempting to AI-wash their products and services will often:
· Overstate their capabilities – implying that their AI models and algorithms are more powerful, useful or flexible than they actually are.
· Misleadingly use the term ‘intelligent’ – when, in fact, the software doesn’t use algorithms capable of learning and making decisions without being explicitly programmed how to do so.
· Offer very vague definitions – Not specifically explaining which elements are ‘intelligent’ and which rely on traditional software methodologies or human input.
· Downplay the amount of human input involved – either on the part of the service provider or the user.
One way of looking at it is that AI washing is like painting ‘go-faster’ stripes on a car without upgrading the engine, allowing marketers to capitalize on the excitement around AI while not offering anything that’s genuinely revolutionary.
Why Is It A Problem?
While it may seem like the kind of harmless marketing bluster we’re all used to in the field of business technology, as with greenwashing it creates some real challenges and risks.
For example, it can stifle or obscure true innovation as real AI breakthroughs struggle to be noticed amid the hype and noise of so many exaggerated claims.
It also erodes consumer trust in AI, as users become cynical about claims made by the industry in general.
It creates challenges for investors, who want to allocate funds to genuinely innovative projects and may miss opportunities to help bring projects that offer real technological advances and value to market.
And it can also lead to inflated expectations around what AI is currently capable of achieving, which could result in businesses setting unrealistic goals and targets.
What Are Some Examples Of AI Washing?
Many home appliances – from fridges and kettles to vacuum cleaners and thermostats, are labeled as ‘smart’ or ‘intelligent’ when they should more accurately be labeled as ‘connected.' Despite being linked to the internet and controllable via apps, they often do not have the capacity to learn or operate autonomously, as is generally expected of AI applications.
Many companies offer tools that they say can automate the process of creating videos, copy and content. In reality, they often require significant human input in order to generate output of an acceptable quality.
For a specific example, Coca-Cola was accused of AI washing for a campaign claiming it had used AI to create a new drink. Although it stated that the Y3000 flavor had been ‘co-created’ with AI, there was no real explanation of how AI was involved in the process. Some critics pointed out that it seemed to be name-dropping AI to make the product seem more innovative than it actually was.
And in the world of finance and investment, two firms were this year charged by the SEC with making ‘false and misleading statements’ regarding the extent to which AI is used to manage their investment strategies.
How To Spot AI Washing In The Wild
Some who are very skeptical about the capabilities and potential of AI will claim that everything called ‘AI’ today is effectively ‘AI washing’, because computers aren’t yet capable of true intelligence.
But for the purposes of this article we are using the definition of AI that’s currently accepted - software tools that can learn how to carry out tasks by being trained on data, rather than explicitly programmed how to do them. This form of real-world, business-focused AI is often referred to as machine learning.
Spotting when companies are trying it on involves developing a skeptical eye for these claims. Look for mentions of specific models, technologies or algorithms that are used, such as natural language processing, neural networks or deep learning. And seek out mentions of ‘transparent’ AI, where companies are open about the types of data and algorithms that are involved.
Beware of companies that seem unwilling or unable to describe how their technology works. Sometimes, this information will be found in case studies or white papers published on corporate websites.
And if you’re dealing with a sales representative, ask them to explain what steps are taken to avoid bias in their data and algorithms, or AI hallucinations. If they don’t have solutions to these problems, it’s possible that they aren’t really using AI at all.
This skepticism is critical for making better decisions about what technology to invest in, as well as contributing towards the development of a more honest and transparent AI landscape in the long-term.

title: Council Post: Four Stories That Will Change Business Texting Forever In 2024
text:
CMO and co-founder of EZ Texting.
Looking further into 2024, big changes coming to text communications are going to have profound effects on marketing, sales and audience experience, from reduced friction and improved security to enhanced features and branding opportunities.
Here's how the coming of AI, the end of third-party cookies, the arrival of RCS and the expansion of OTT opportunities are going to change texting forever.
1. RCS Redraws The Text Marketing Playbook
Perhaps the greatest impact on text communications in 2024 will come from Apple’s adoption of RCS, which is currently slated for summer.
While much of the world is already using RCS (rich communication system) as the standard replacement for SMS—Juniper Research says global RCS users will reach 1.1 billion in 2024, rising from 930 million in 2023—Apple’s dominance and reliance on its proprietary iMessage system has meant that RCS adoption has been restricted to Android devices. No more!
The move from Apple—staving off inquiries into the company's ongoing interoperability issues—will finally address any ongoing blue-bubble/green-bubble drama in your life, as well as open up a whole new world of texting benefits.
Businesses will be able to exert more control over their brands and text communications than with SMS, as RCS allows for longer messages, larger files, more videos and images, group conversations, and cross-app connectivity.
Anyone who has written off texting and SMS as dusty tech with few capabilities should prepare to take another look. Changes coming with RCS include but are not limited to:
• Custom colors and branding.
• In-text call-to-action buttons.
• In-text image carousels.
• Enhanced security with verified sender IDs.
• Group text conversations.
2. AI Will Make Businesses More Productive And More Responsive
Yes, AI is everywhere.
Yes, it’s going to change things.
It already is.
My company recently rolled out two SMS-based generative AI features, and we’re already seeing AI improve productivity, personalization, accuracy, response times and contact and close rates for our customers.
Two areas in which we’ve seen AI have the greatest impact are sales and customer service. A recent InsiderIntelligence study found similar results, with the bulk of organizations surveyed (47%) already using generative AI, saying they use it most for sales and customer service.
Our recent 2024 Consumer Texting Behavior Report found that consumers continue to check and respond to their messages faster than ever—and they expect the same speed from the businesses they interact with.
The marriage of AI to text messaging’s mobile, push notification nature allows for that speed in an asynchronous environment—and for businesses using text to respond to incoming leads and customer support concerns faster.
3. Goodbye, Third-Party Cookies; Hello, First-Party Data
Digital marketing was virtually built on third-party cookies, allowing businesses to build targeted campaigns based on user behavior data. Due to a shifting privacy landscape, Apple began blocking third-party cookies in 2021, and with Google starting to block cookies this January, it looks like 2024 is the last stand for the resilient trackers.
Instead of mourning the crumbling of the third-party cookie, brands need to look to new tools and strategies to understand their customers at scale and build targeted campaigns, including website data, social media, email engagement, and text communication.
At my company, we’ve always viewed text as an incredibly personal form of communication, which makes it beyond valuable in better understanding your audience. And with the coming advancements of RCS that allow for greater conversational, branding and conversion opportunities, you can keep your audience in your texting window with no need for a third party.
Link data, polls, quizzes, surveys, and feedback or review requests are all ways to use texts to collect valuable first-party data from your audience in an organic and engaging way.
4. OTT Puts Over 3 Billion Customers In Play
The popularity of OTT messaging apps—WhatsApp, Meta’s Messenger and Google Messenger, among others—continues to grow. With numbers too big to ignore, we’ll see more channels and CRMs integrating OTT standards and capabilities in order to meet audiences where they live—their phones.
With Apple finally establishing RCS standards along with the release of iOS 18 in June, there remain other OTT (over-the-top) walled gardens that the text industry needs to scale to ensure consistent communications across touchpoints for our customers.
Our recent survey found that text has become the preferred channel for consumers across a wide variety of use cases, including customer support. Couple an audience of over 3 billion strong to consumer demand for the ability to text businesses and organizations across a wide variety of use cases, and it’s easy to see the need for solutions.
Multichannel inboxes will allow for flexible communication as the drive to deliver OTT audiences will power a deeper integration of text into omnichannel strategies, offering even greater insights into customer data.
Chatbot and e-commerce integrations, improved personalization, richer media and, in some cases, higher levels of security, such as Whatsapp’s end-to-end encryption, are all benefits that will be driven by changes in consumer behavior, technology and the communications landscape. In the end, OTT’s reach and flexibility might be enough to break the necessity of the Web for many brands.

AI spending worries cast gloom over Alphabet, Microsoft
During Meta's earnings conference call, analysts peppered CEO Mark Zuckerberg with questions about how the company was pacing its AI investments. One analyst asked whether Meta was spending more because it saw an even bigger opportunity from AI.
By Sheila Dang
Investors appear to be losing patience with Big Tech's prodigious artificial intelligence investments this week after Meta Platforms signaled deeper spending and a long road to profitability.
The concession from Meta in its quarterly report late on Wednesday cast a cloud over Microsoft and Alphabet, which will both report quarterly earnings on Thursday.
Meta's stock sank 15% in extended trade after it forecast higher AI spending next year, while Microsoft was down 2%, Alphabet fell 3% and Nvidia dropped 1.4% in reaction.
Wall Street's heavyweight tech-related companies have been locked in a fierce battle to advance generative AI, which can create text, videos and photos from prompts and is seen as the next frontier in tech.
During Meta's earnings conference call, analysts peppered CEO Mark Zuckerberg with questions about how the company was pacing its AI investments. One analyst asked whether Meta was spending more because it saw an even bigger opportunity from AI.
"I think we've gotten more ambitious and optimistic on AI," Zuckerberg responded, pointing to Meta's recent launches of new AI models. "So all of that basically encourages me to make sure that we're investing to stay at the leading edge of this."
Alphabet and Microsoft both said earlier this year when they reported fourth-quarter results that they expected rising AI costs. The investor reaction on Wednesday indicated deepening concerns.
In a research note on Monday about Alphabet, analysts from New Street Research said the potential for materially higher capital expenditures was a worry ahead of results on Thursday.
The research firm said it now expects Alphabet's full-year capital expenditures to be $45.9 billion, up from its previous estimate of $42.7 billion.
Google has been working to catch up in the generative AI race and released Gemini, a model that can understand and create different types of information including text, audio and video.
Creating content with generative AI is energy-intensive, and Zuckerberg cited the cost as a reason for Meta's higher expenses.
Meanwhile, Microsoft has positioned itself to be a winner in AI due to its partnership with OpenAI, which kicked off the generative AI craze last year with ChatGPT, said analysts from Jefferies in a note on March 31.
Microsoft has integrated chatbots into its suite of Office products and is planning to invest more in data centers.
Industry-wide, shareholders are now focused on looking for revenue, including pricing models and whether customers can find use cases that justify the cost of generative AI, Jefferies wrote.
"Last year was spent dreaming of gen AI's potential," the analysts wrote. "This year will be about moving forward with concrete steps."

title: Council Post: Strategies For Responsible AI Implementation
text:
Venkat, CEO & Founder of 10decoders, drives SMB's growth with Strategy & Consulting.
In today's digital landscape, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a powerful tool driving innovation and transformation across industries. However, with its pervasive influence comes uncharted ethical waters to navigate. From legal compliance to societal impact, I believe that the deployment of AI demands a comprehensive approach toward responsible practices.
In my experience, achieving AI readiness involves more than just mastering the technology; it requires a transformative shift in your organizational culture—one that welcomes change and can overcome misconceptions and anxieties surrounding AI.
As touched on earlier, when creating this culture, companies must also build the groundwork to navigate the intricate ethical issues linked to AI use. This includes creating clear policies and frameworks for ethical AI practices as well as encouraging transparent conversations within the workplace.
Below I would like to explore the journey toward responsible AI by focusing on three key areas: Ethical alignment, accountability infrastructure and bias detection and mitigation.
Ethical Alignment: Setting The Compass Right
At the heart of responsible AI lies the alignment of business values with ethical principles. I believe that businesses should establish clear guidelines that prioritize legality, data privacy and social impact in their AI endeavors. As you create these guidelines for the development and deployment of AI tools, ensure that all stakeholders are aware of and committed to upholding these principles.
Building these policies, though, poses specific challenges like the need to reconcile profit motives with ethical standards as well as ensuring data privacy and security without compromising operational efficiency.
To help overcome these hurdles, in my company, we employ techniques like rule-set evolution to help clarify and guide our decision-making processes. Prioritizing the development of specific rules that can detect and quantify biases in AI models helps to ensure fair outcomes.
Accountability Infrastructure: Building The Foundation
To operationalize responsible AI, businesses need to establish a robust accountability infrastructure. This involves assigning roles and responsibilities across the organization to oversee AI governance and compliance with ethical standards.
I suggest establishing a clear framework that assigns specific roles and responsibilities across all levels: Executives, AI ethics boards, project managers, developers and auditors.
For example, in my company, we have adopted a framework that mandates every employee have clear documentation of their AI decision-making processes. This includes detailing the data used and algorithms applied, making it easier for stakeholders to understand how solutions are derived.
We have also established a dedicated team responsible for regularly auditing AI models to help identify any potential biases and ensure these tools adhere to ethical standards and regulations. Moreover, effective communication strategies include regular training sessions, workshops and knowledge-sharing sessions.
Bias Detection And Mitigation: Striving For Fairness
Bias can manifest in various forms including algorithmic biases, data biases and cultural biases.
I find that one of the most important aspects of bias mitigation is the use of diverse datasets that are more representative of the target population. This approach ensures models are equitable and outcomes are fair across all groups. It also helps identify and correct biases early in the development process.
Pioneering Continuous Improvement In AI Deployment
As noted, it is important to proactively address emerging challenges. Past fostering a culture of learning and iteration within your organization, look to also stay abreast of developments in AI ethics, regulations and best practices. This allows you to adjust your strategies and policies accordingly.
An illustrative example of a company adapting its AI ethics strategy is IBM, which decided to withdraw from the general-purpose facial recognition market in 2020. This decision came amid growing concerns about bias and the potential misuse of technology in law enforcement and surveillance.
IBM recognized the ethical implications and societal impacts of facial recognition technology, leading them to reassess their position and focus on developing AI in a more responsible and transparent manner. I see this pivot underscoring the importance of aligning AI development with ethical standards and societal values.
Key Takeaways
The journey toward responsible AI requires a holistic approach that encompasses ethical alignment, continuous improvement, accountability infrastructure, bias detection and mitigation. As AI continues to evolve, I urge businesses to remain vigilant in their efforts to navigate these ethical waters and ensure that their AI serves the greater good of society.

title: Council Post: Why It’s The Year Of Proprietary Data, Not AI
text:
Co-founder of Gulp Data, a provider of data valuations, data-backed loans, and data monetization services.
This year has been hailed as the year of artificial intelligence (AI) breakthroughs. The exponential growth of AI, from OpenAI to chatbots and self-driving cars, boasts of a future where machines are not just intelligent but autonomous. While numerous articles extensively cover AI integration, societal impact and engineering challenges, they overlook a critical aspect.
Beneath the surface of AI innovation lies a pivotal, albeit overlooked, element: proprietary data. Contrary to the prevailing narrative, the true catalyst for AI progress is not solely the sophistication of algorithms or computing power but rather access to vast quantities of data, exceptionally high-quality proprietary data.
This assertion rests on two fundamental pillars: legal implications of data ownership and the significance of unique, proprietary data.
1. Legal Implications Of Data Ownership And Ethical Data Gathering
There is no doubt that data is the core ingredient fueling the engines of AI innovation, but the landscape of data ownership is fraught with legal and ethical complexities. Companies grapple with data sovereignty, privacy concerns and the ethics of data acquisition.
While copyright laws delineate ownership rights, they lag behind the rapid evolution of AI, leaving gray areas in data use. Moreover, unethical data-gathering mechanisms, such as web scraping, cast shadows over the legitimacy and further blur the lines surrounding data use. We are already witnessing a wave of lawsuits and complaints revolving around data gathering and ownership. In just the past 12 months, Getty Images sued AI art generator Stable Diffusion, The New York Times sued OpenAI for copyright infringement and Meta sued Bright Data for data scraping.
Various news outlets recently sued OpenAI for misuse of their articles, and a group of authors filed a class action against the AI giant, claiming they used their content to train ChatGPT. These concerns are significantly mitigated when dealing with first-party and second-party data. This direct relationship between the data collector and the user allows for clear documentation of consent, making it easier to demonstrate compliance with privacy laws and reducing the risk of unauthorized collection.
Those racing to build the best AI must license data directly from the companies that generate it. A recent notable example was when Reddit signed a $60 million-per-year deal with Google to make its content available for training Google’s AI. Proprietary data safeguards against legal entanglements such as lawsuits and copyright infringements and fosters the development of differentiated technologies.
2. Access To Proprietary Data: The Decisive Factor
Racing To The Same Point
In the race toward AI supremacy, access to data is the ultimate differentiator. While open-source and scraped datasets provide a foundational framework for AI development, they often lack specificity, depth and exclusivity. As a result, companies find themselves converging on similar technological capabilities, leading to a homogenized market devoid of differentiation.
While the proliferation of open-source data is cost-effective and time-efficient, the real winners in the AI landscape will be those who secure access to the most comprehensive and proprietary datasets—the data that their competitors don’t have access to. These exclusive datasets encapsulate the nuances of specific industries, populations and data types, creating a foundation that is not only different from their competitors but at a lower risk of bias, disinformation and inaccurate training data.
Risk Of Introducing Bias
As AI-generated content becomes increasingly prevalent, we risk entering a technological Ouroboros scenario, where AI systems are both creators and consumers of biased content. Internet-sourced large language models (LLMs) are susceptible to bias and inaccuracies due to their reliance on massive open-source training data. Furthermore, as AI-generated content proliferates on the internet, these LLMs may inadvertently perpetuate biases in the content they consume. It is imperative to integrate new, proprietary data sources with higher-quality training data to mitigate this risk and ensure the trustworthiness of AI systems.
That's why this is not the year of AI advancement but rather the year of proprietary data. Legal frameworks and ethical considerations surrounding data ownership and acquisition are pivotal in shaping the trajectory of AI progress. Access to proprietary datasets emerges as the decisive factor separating the front-runners from the laggards in the AI race. This leads us to an exciting place—an opportunity for companies to participate in data monetization, creating new lines of revenue by licensing data critical to the blossoming AI market.

title: Council Post: Operationalizing AI: 5 Steps To Maximize The Impact Of AI Investments
text:
Scott Zoldi, Chief Analytics Officer, FICO.
“Software is eating the world,” venture capitalist Marc Andreessen famously declared in 2011. Today, it’s clear that artificial intelligence (AI) is now eating the world—spurred on by organizations’ insatiable appetite for all flavors of this breakthrough technology, including generative AI (GenAI). But amidst the avalanche of rosy predictions about how much money organizations will invest in enterprise AI solutions and the productivity gains they expect to achieve, a small footnote of a statistic from McKinsey & Co. stands out: Less than 10% of companies are able to generate AI impact at scale.
The main reason most AI deployments will fail to deliver meaningful impact is their haphazard implementation by non-data scientists, without appropriate forethought, structure, processes or guardrails. For artificial intelligence technology to have a chance of succeeding in the enterprise, AI must be operationalized.
What Is Operationalization?
The term operationalization has its roots in quantitative research methods, where it means “turning abstract conceptual ideas into measurable observations.” In enterprise technology circles, operationalization is the analogous process by which any given technology, such as AI-based decisioning, is implemented in a repeatable, measurable way—an optimized combination of people, process and technology.
In my role as Chief Analytics Officer at FICO, where I lead a team of more than 100 data scientists at the forefront of AI innovation, I have developed five principles that always form the framework of any analytics deployment.
Five Steps To Operationalize AI
1. Start with a world-class team: Putting domain experts in charge may sound like a “brief glimpse of the obvious,” but would you have an IT engineer head up a high-visibility customer-facing marketing campaign? Probably not. Yet that is exactly what has happened with lightning-fast GenAI deployments, in particular—remember the airline customer service team that put a GenAI chatbot in charge of dispensing refund information? Or the lawyer who asked ChatGPT to write a legal brief?
AI technology is powerful, with the potential to do both great good and catastrophic harm. As such, its deployment needs to be strategized and delivered with the utmost care by world-class data science professionals with not just the proper academic credentials but the real-world experience to correctly apply AI to solve business problems, which are always more complex than they seem on the surface.
2. Invent AI to meet the target industry or need: As a corollary beyond the data science team, the entire organization must be focused on using AI solutions for high-value business problems. This includes first quantifying the business need; often, addressing it will require inventing new algorithms, not just relying on “vanilla” AI solutions such as open source libraries and off-the-shelf GenAI large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, Llama, Gemini and others.
However, in their excitement to realize the tantalizing, if dubious, transformative benefits of AI (such as an estimated $4.4 trillion annual global productivity boost, slightly more than the entire gross domestic product [GDP] of Germany), many firms are quickly launching a multitude of experimental projects typically powered by “vanilla” AI and GenAI. The inherent lack of application-specific invention, governance and control over such a scattershot approach translates into wasted resources and longer time to value.
3. Build AI algorithms for efficient software deployment: The hallmark challenge of operationalizing AI is a persistent mentality of siloed functions; in many organizations, data scientists throw AI models over a metaphorical fence to a software development team that has little to no ability to deploy them.
Successful AI deployment requires machine learning/AI scientists to be involved in the software design process, providing requirements and understanding the constraints being applied to their algorithms. This approach limits the inherent impedance mismatch between analytic scientists and software developers, instead setting up the necessary design constraints under which successful AI solutions are developed.
4. Deliver low-latency, high-throughput execution: Well-architected cloud computing resources are capable of operationalizing AI decisioning systems to meet business needs. In production environment this can typically include real-time response, which requires careful understanding of the entire chain of data flow, preprocessing, streaming analytics, NoSQL storage, system redundancy and other assets.
For example, an AI system to detect payment card fraud must deliver single-digit millisecond response times. (In comparison, the blink of an eye is about 300 milliseconds.) Meeting this service level agreement (SLA) requires a meticulously architected, highly scalable cloud infrastructure to support purpose-optimized AI algorithms.
5. Relentlessly pursue Responsible AI: For artificial intelligence technology to provide business value, it must be ethical, explainable and auditable. These are the key concepts of Responsible AI, a set of principles and practices to operationalize AI deployments that deliver high-impact business results within important ethical and legal boundaries.
Moreover, with artificial intelligence regulation ramping up over the globe, operationalization must include the ability to demonstrate compliance with AI regulatory standards. This is facilitated by the tenets of accountability and explainability that are central to responsible AI and can be achieved by using immutable blockchain technology to codify every aspect of AI model development, using the same AI governance blockchain to define how AI operates in production and is monitored.
Ultimately, operationalizing AI is a greater challenge than traditional enterprise software design and deployment; Responsible AI and customer trust add multiple layers of complexity to solve. By following these five steps, organizations across industries can break down that complexity—and operationalize innovative AI solutions that can deliver maximum business impact.

title: 5 ChatGPT Prompts To Increase Your Sales
text:
The AI revolution isn’t coming—it’s here, and businesses can’t afford to ignore or fear it. Instead of viewing AI as a disruptor threatening to take your or your team members’ jobs, you can see it as another powerful productivity tool to incorporate into your workflows. Just consider a notoriously difficult area like sales. As a business owner, I understand the challenge of moving the needle. Research backs me up—a Harvard Business Review study of over 1,200 B2B companies found that just one in 20 companies consistently grew sales faster than sales and marketing expenses.
ChatGPT and plenty of other AI tools can help talented sales teams to work smarter, not harder, removing some of the busywork from their plates to focus on more meaningful aspects of their jobs—as I call it, the “big stuff.” Or, if you’re a bootstrapper just beginning your entrepreneurial journey, and yet to have a sales team, ChatGPT can be a powerful, cost-effective tool to jumpstart your sales. Here are five prompts to consider.
1. Revamp your sales goals
Revisiting and clarifying your sales goals is the first step in boosting your bottom line. Maybe your company doesn’t have clear sales goals. Or they’ve gradually lost sight of them. Over time, the daily grind tends to blur our long-term objectives, but they should be at the forefront of your mind, guiding your work each day.
Goals should be specific—concrete and measurable. The following ChatGPT prompt can serve as an actionable guide for fleshing out your sales goals:
“My [industry] company would like to boost its sales. First, we want to clarify our sales goals. Can you provide 10 questions to help our sales team create concrete, measurable sales goals?”
A rule of thumb when using ChatGPT: the more context you provide—background information about your company, its products or services, industry, any unique challenges, etc—the more helpful the answers will be.
2. Refine your target market
Understanding your target market is critical for tailoring your sales messaging and communicating more effectively. According to one study, 68 percent of consumers expect personalization every time they reach out to a company. Identifying and continually refining your target audience will help you to connect in a personalized way.
The following prompt can generate a productive brainstorm:
“My [industry] company serves [current target market] in [geographic location]. We would like to clarify our target market. Can you ask 10 questions to help me determine the best target market(s) to boost sales?”
The idea isn’t just to search and find the answers, but to get the wheels turning so that salespeople discover the answers on their own. Once you hone in on your target markets, you can use ChatGPT to edit your messaging—emails, social media posts, etc.—to ensure that it’s sufficiently tailored to them.
3. Unify your customer-facing brand
Nowadays, a company’s voice is integral to its brand. That voice should be consistent, from website content to blog posts to sales scripts. ChatGPT can familiarize itself with your company’s voice and ensure that sales messaging is consistent, presenting a unified front across your company. You just need to submit text that captures the brand voice and ask ChatGPT to tweak your text accordingly. Consider a version of the following prompt:
“I want you to analyze the following text from my company’s [website, blog, etc], beginning and ending in quotes. [“Insert text here”] Then, I want you to review the text below, a [content] from one of our sales representatives, and edit it so that the voice and tone match.”
Once you submit the above prompt, ChatGPT will (politely) request the relevant text. For example, when I tested the above prompt, it replied, “Sure, please provide the email text from your sales representative, and I'll review it to ensure the voice and tone match the quoted text from your company's website. Once I have the email text, I'll be able to make the necessary edits.”
4. Crunch the numbers
When it comes to landing a sale, the more you understand your numbers, the more you can improve the sales process. That means gathering data and analyzing it from as many angles as possible. ChatGPT can step in to analyze your data and help come up with ideas to improve the results. For example, if you notice that prospects are failing to make it past a certain phase of the sales funnel, you can submit an organized data set to ChatGPT to understand where they’re falling off and why that might be happening. The prompt could be:
“I want you to analyze the following data set showing my company’s leads throughout the sales funnel. Can you generate ideas about why leads are not converting into customers?”
Be sure to explain the data you’re submitting and the specific insight you’re after.
5. Ongoing training
Learning and development are critical parts of any sales job in today’s quickly evolving, increasingly AI-fueled workplace. But the buck doesn’t stop at teaching employees how to use AI—that would give short shrift to the technology’s full potential. As Harvard Business Review notes, you can make training sessions a live practice.
For example, give sales reps customer scenarios and have them brainstorm potential solutions. Then, you can use ChatGPT to understand what objections a potential customer might have. So, rather than using generative AI like an editor or a search engine, you’re engaging in hypothetical dialogues, potentially expanding and sharpening your thinking.
Here’s a template for this type of prompt:
“I’m a salesperson at a [description] company, looking to offer a potential customer a solution for their [issue]. The customer is [insert description]. Their issue is [description]. Please review the following proposed solution and generate any objections the customer may have.”
In mere seconds, ChatGPT will generate a list of potential concerns that a salesperson can think through and prepare for.
Generative AI is the mainland, not the frontier. Sales teams can integrate tools like ChatGPT into their workflows to tackle busywork, spark creativity, and experiment with potential uses as AI capabilities continue to expand.

title: Council Post: Rethinking Brand Management On E-Commerce Marketplaces
text:
Hai Mag is the co-founder and CEO of Eva, Profit Maximization Software and Agency Services for Amazon and all Marketplaces.
In the ever-evolving e-commerce space, brands face an important choice when it comes to managing their presence on platforms such as Amazon: whether to rely on in-house teams or outsource to digital marketing agencies. At the same time, as technology advances, a brand-new paradigm has emerged.
Traditionally, agencies largely deal with market operations and provide strategies for growth and assistance. However, I believe these dynamics are changing with the emergence of technologies powered by artificial intelligence. For example, campaign bid optimization can be done hourly by AI instead of daily or weekly updates by an agency.
This raises many questions: Can technology take over all the tasks performed by an agency or an in-house team? What would be the most optimized way to manage e-commerce operations? In this article, I propose a new model: Brands can harness artificial intelligence, strategic orchestration and human expertise to efficiently navigate the complexities of online retail.
Maximizing Market Success: Integrating AI And Human Expertise
While AI tools provide remarkable capabilities, they have also shown us that they often lack the contextual knowledge and strategic insight inherent in human expertise. The most effective and ideal way to solve this is to integrate AI with human judgment. By doing so, brands can optimize their market techniques, benefit from the efficiency of automation and maintain the ability to make subtle choices based on human expertise.
To give an example, while AI can optimize campaign creation and bid optimization processes, people can analyze competitive information and create offensive or defensive strategies. Agile in-house teams can analyze the outcomes and ensure product features are better optimized to outsmart the competition and better targeted for the right customer segment.
Brands can already start internally using generative AI applications to help them generate more relevant content on social media or create and localize listings for omnichannel e-commerce platforms. Third-party services powered by AI can also be explored for pricing, inventory management and advertising. (Full disclosure: My company provides these types of solutions, as do others.) Brand leaders can encourage their teams to explore uses for AI. However, it’s also important to make it clear that AI is not intended to replace employees.
Getting your e-commerce team on board with AI isn’t just about throwing new tools at them and hoping for the best. It’s about a mindset shift, and it’s going to be a journey. Think of it as a three-part adventure:
1. Adoption: This is where the rubber meets the road. Your team might grumble a bit at first; new tools can feel like just another thing to learn. But here’s where you step in as a leader. Keep encouraging them, show them how these AI tools can make their day-to-day easier, and make sure everyone gets the training they need. It’s all about showing the value, not just telling them about it.
2. Acceptance. This is the fun part. As your team gets more comfortable, they’ll start to see what AI can really do. They’ll probably even get a bit excited thinking about all the stuff they won’t have to do manually anymore. But they’ll also start to see where AI doesn’t quite cut it.
3. Appreciation. This is when your team really starts to get it. They’ll see where their human skills outshine what AI can do. They’ll understand how to blend their talents with AI to do even better work—especially for those tasks that need a human touch, like creative problem-solving or connecting with customers.
Working With Consultants
Brands looking to use AI might consider working with agencies or AI consultants to help them scale faster and more efficiently. However, before working with such companies, brands need to consider their technology needs and the agency or consultant’s expertise. The main challenges I’ve found in the e-commerce space are traffic, conversion, availability and profitability. These are interdependent, and I believe technologies and teams that aim to holistically address these issues will perform the best.
From my perspective, the ongoing dilemma between in-house teams and agencies does not properly address the complexities of AI in managing market operations. Brands can evaluate a third alternative and consider working with technology companies that can help them embrace AI while training their own agile teams to be more AI-compatible.

title: Council Post: Key C-Suite Discussions That Would Benefit From Tech Leaders’ Takes
text:

Today’s tech executives have embraced an expanded role. They welcome sharing their specialized knowledge to help the leadership team make fully informed decisions on a variety of issues and helping out with essential functions that can benefit from their unique experience. title: Council Post: The Rise Of Specialized AI Assistants
text:
Ardis Kadiu, Founder & CEO at Element451, Host of Generation AI Podcast.
Just as we wonder how we lived without mobile phones, I believe we’ll do the same with AI assistants in a few years. Remember when you had to delete emails and schedule meetings on your calendar manually? Looking back, it will be hard to ignore all the times we spent on the same tasks, day after day.
We’re seeing new generative AI tools and solutions rolling out practically every day. Until now, AI systems have been primarily designed to be general-purpose and capable of performing a wide range of tasks across different domains. Although these generalist AI systems have undoubtedly provided value, they’re limited in how much they can do. As a result, businesses and institutions are starting to use specialized AI assistants that can leverage domain-specific knowledge and skills to deliver more targeted and practical support.
Understanding The Benefits
We’ve seen a flurry of new AI assistants introduced this year, including Devin, Cognition AI’s software development assistant. There’s been a lot of focus on developer assistants for a while, and the level of sophistication is encouraging. But software developers aren’t the only ones benefiting from having an AI assistant.
As this technology becomes more pervasive, there's a growing recognition of the need for AI assistants tailored to support specific roles and tasks within industries. These specialized, expert AI assistants are trained to complete specific tasks based on the unique needs of the employees they assist, marking a significant shift in how AI is utilized in the workplace.
For example, the healthcare industry may require AI assistants trained to interpret medical imaging scans or assist with patient diagnosis. At the same time, the financial sector may benefit from AI assistants that can analyze complex market data and make informed investment decisions.
By developing specialized AI assistants, businesses and institutions can harness the power of technology to address specific pain points and capitalize on opportunities unique to their industry. These assistants can be trained using large datasets and advanced deep-learning techniques to acquire the specialized knowledge and skills to perform their tasks precisely and accurately.
Specialized AI assistants can enhance productivity and efficiency by automating repetitive tasks and freeing human employees to focus on more high-value activities. In customer service, AI assistants can handle routine inquiries and provide basic support, allowing human agents to dedicate their time to resolving complex issues and delivering personalized service.
Another advantage is their ability to adapt and evolve to meet changing demands and circumstances. Through continuous learning and refinement, these assistants can stay up to date with the latest developments in their respective fields and continuously improve their performance.
Addressing The Challenges
However, developing and deploying specialized AI assistants also presents challenges and considerations that must be addressed. One such challenge is the need for high-quality domain-specific data that accurately reflects the complexities of the task. With sufficient and relevant data, AI assistants may be able to perform effectively, highlighting the importance of data collection and curation efforts.
Ethical and privacy concerns also surround using AI assistants, particularly in industries involving sensitive information. Businesses and institutions must ensure that proper safeguards are in place to protect the confidentiality and integrity of data handled by AI assistants and that their use complies with relevant regulations and guidelines.
Despite these challenges, the adoption of specialized AI assistants is poised to grow as businesses and institutions recognize their value in addressing industry-specific needs and driving innovation.
Managing The Digital Team Of The Future
It’s likely that AI assistants will eventually play a role in practically every organization. So, as we look out a year or two and companies amass assistants across functions and roles, it’s clear that our assistants will need to “work” with one another.
Consider a marketing team that uses various assistants for design, copywriting, campaigns and events. The work doesn’t all happen simultaneously; it’s sequential, with some occurring in parallel. That means the assistants need to communicate with one another.
Also, my company provides AI assistants to higher education institutions, and as we talk to universities, there’s tremendous excitement for AI, particularly when it comes to managing events, financial aid advising and campaign strategy. It makes sense for higher education to adopt AI assistants, given challenges with staffing, growing competition for enrollment and students' rising expectations.
Although AI assistants will never replace the human touch, they can enhance efficiency and streamline operations. Working behind the scenes in very specific roles, they act as indispensable team members.

title: 5 Key Economic Impacts And Strategic Implications Of AI For Leaders
text:
The economic impacts of Artificial Intelligence (AI) are not just significant, but also complex, influencing various aspects from individual firms to global financial structures. Understanding these impacts is crucial for business leaders as it can guide their decision-making and help them adapt to the evolving business landscape. Strategically, AI acts as a catalyst for innovation and a disruptive force, reshaping industries and altering competitive dynamics. A leader should know the following 5 economic impacts and strategic implications of AI.
1. Productivity Enhancement:
AI technologies enhance productivity through automation, analytics, and process optimization. They enable businesses to perform more tasks with fewer errors and in less time, often transcending human capabilities in speed and accuracy. This reduces costs and frees up human resources for higher-value activities, potentially leading to higher overall productivity within the economy. For example, AI-driven supply chain management systems can predict inventory requirements and optimize logistics, significantly reducing overhead costs and improving service delivery.
2. Employment and Labor Markets:
The impact of AI on employment is complex and dual-faceted. While AI can lead to job displacement, particularly in routine and repetitive roles, it also creates new jobs that require more advanced skills, such as AI system maintenance, data analysis, and the development of new AI technologies. The net effect on employment varies by industry. It can depend on factors such as the speed of AI adoption and the flexibility of the labor market. Business leaders need to consider these dynamics as they integrate AI technologies, planning strategically for workforce transitions and upskilling programs.
3. Innovation and Competitive Advantage:
AI drives innovation by enabling the development of new products and services and by enhancing the capabilities of existing ones. For instance, in the healthcare sector, AI algorithms can analyze vast amounts of medical data to assist in diagnosing diseases earlier and more accurately than ever before. This improves patient outcomes and provides healthcare businesses with a competitive edge in the market.
4. Market Structures and Firm Strategy:
AI affects market structures by lowering entry barriers in some industries while increasing the scale economies in others. This can lead to greater market concentration in sectors where AI significantly enhances productivity, as larger firms can better invest in costly AI technologies. Consequently, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) may find competing challenging unless they adopt innovative strategies or collaborate in ecosystems that can democratize access to AI resources.
5. Decision Making:
AI transforms strategic decision-making by providing leaders with insights derived from data analysis that were previously unavailable or difficult to obtain. AI's predictive capabilities allow businesses to accurately anticipate market trends, consumer behavior, and potential risks. This strategic foresight is critical in fast-moving sectors where early detection of shifts can be a significant competitive advantage.
Strategic Implications for Leaders:
For business leaders, the strategic implications of AI are not just challenges, but also opportunities. They have the potential to harness AI's transformative power, adapting to an environment where integrating and leveraging AI is a key determinant of success. This involves technological adoption and a holistic approach to fostering an AI-ready culture that embraces continuous learning and ethical considerations. By taking the lead in this transformation, business leaders can shape the future of their industries and drive their organizations to new heights.
Moreover, leaders must not only adapt, but also lead the way in navigating the evolving regulatory landscape to address the unique challenges posed by AI, including privacy concerns, ethical data use, and transparency in AI decision-making processes. Strategic planning and collaboration will be the key to success in the AI era, suggesting that collaboration among businesses, governments, and educational institutions will be crucial. This is not a choice, but a necessity for businesses to thrive in the AI era.

In today's digital age, Artificial Intelligence (AI) is not just a technological innovation but a transformative strategic asset that can catapult businesses to unprecedented levels of efficiency, Innovation, and market leadership. As AI becomes more integral to business operations, maintaining ethical standards becomes paramount. This includes addressing issues like privacy, bias in AI algorithms, and the social implications of automation.

Collaborating with technology providers, research institutions, and other organizations can provide access to advanced AI tools and innovations, facilitating more effective implementation.
AI as a strategic asset offers substantial benefits across multiple facets of business operations, from improving efficiency and customer engagement to driving Innovation and managing risk. By strategically integrating AI, leaders cannot only achieve specific business objectives but also position their organizations as pioneers in the digital era, fostering a sense of strategic foresight and forward-thinking.

title: Tech Stocks Tumble As Meta’s AI Bet Spooks Investors
text:
Topline
Tech stocks tumbled in premarket trading Thursday after lackluster forecasts from Facebook parent Meta spooked investors across the sector, a sign that Wall Street’s willingness to embrace artificial intelligence may not match the seemingly boundless enthusiasm of Silicon Valley.
Key Facts
Meta shares plummeted more than 15% during premarket trading after the company told investors to expect slower growth and big spending on AI moving forward, as there isn’t a clear path for how the technology would become a money-maker for the firm, which almost exclusively makes its money through ads.
The downturn sparked a wider selloff of major tech stocks, including Google parent Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, which all fell between 2% and 3% during premarket hours.
Social media firms Snap and Pinterest also fell between 4% and 5%, with recently-floated Reddit suffering a less dramatic slip of around 1%.
Chip maker Nvidia, which makes hardware vital for building AI systems and saw its value soar earlier this year amid the technology’s boom, initially fell around 2% during premarket trading but had largely recovered as markets approached opening.
Apple and Tesla were generally spared by the broader downturn, with software maker Palantir and hardware maker Dell also falling between 2% and 3%.
The fall comes ahead of more tech earnings Thursday as titans Microsoft, Alphabet and Intel will report.
News Peg
Meta, like many tech companies, has moved swiftly to embrace what has become Silicon Valley’s latest gold rush: generative AI. While AI has long been touted as a transformative and disruptive technology, the launch of OpenAI’s ChatGPT in 2022 marked a milestone for systems that could be trained to generate unique content like text, images, video and sound based on a prompt. The chatbot proved a hit with consumers and sparked intense enthusiasm for the technology, catapulting giants like Google, Microsoft, Meta and Amazon into an AI arms race to reveal, improve and invest in their own AI products. The tech titans, alongside a host of startups like Anthropic, Mistral and Inflection AI, have since produced and released an increasingly powerful array of systems. They show little sign of slowing down, even though a road to profitability through AI is not always clear. Meta released its AI assistant, Meta AI, as a standalone tool last week. The bot, which complements its in-app tools on platforms like WhatsApp and Instagram, is driven by its powerful open source AI model, Llama 3, and is a clear effort to compete with standalone bots from other market leaders like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Alphabet’s Gemini.
Crucial Quote
“You all know our product development playbook by this point,” Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg told investors on Wednesday, attempting to soothe investors by referencing the company’s historic process of releasing a new product, building an audience and scaling it before monetizing it. “There are several ways to build a massive business here,” Zuckerberg said, noting that this has happened with products like Reels, Stories and transitioning News Feed to mobile. With time, Zuckerberg said he is confident this will happen with Meta AI as well, but warned it would take time for these investments to bear fruit. “Realistically, even with shifting many of our existing resources to focus on AI, we'll still grow our investment envelope meaningfully before we make much revenue from some of these new products,” Zuckerberg said.
Tangent
Shares of IBM tumbled nearly 9% during premarket trading. The company unveiled uninspiring sales figures during its earnings report on Wednesday.
Forbes Valuation
Zuckerberg is worth an estimated $173.1 billion. His fortune, a large portion of which comes from his founding stake in Meta’s precursor, Facebook, makes him the fourth richest person in the world, behind Bernard Arnault, Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk, with whom he has publicly feuded and agreed to fight in a cage match. Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, have pledged to give away 99% of their Meta stake within their lifetimes.

Toyota and Nissan pair up with Tencent and Baidu for China AI arms race
The separate announcements from two of Japan's biggest automakers at the Beijing auto show also underscored the attempt by Japanese manufacturers to come to grips with the massive technological shifts that have disrupted their once enviable positions in the Chinese market.
Japan's Toyota Motor will pair up with China's Tencent while Nissan will team up with Baidu, the companies said on Thursday, cross-border partnerships that highlight the importance of artificial intelligence for carmakers.
The separate announcements from two of Japan's biggest automakers at the Beijing auto show also underscored the attempt by Japanese manufacturers to come to grips with the massive technological shifts that have disrupted their once enviable positions in the Chinese market.
Just a few years ago, Japanese car companies were some of the most prominent foreign brands in China. More recently, they have been left flatfooted as local manufacturers led by BYD have snatched market share with software-laden electric vehicles aimed at younger drivers.
Both Tencent, a gaming and social media giant and Baidu, China's leading search engine, have been leaders in the country's generative AI race.
Toyota, the world's largest carmaker by volume, will include technology from tech giant Tencent technology in a China-made passenger vehicle that will go on sale this year, said Toyota's Yiming Xu, a director for brand and communications for China.
The companies will offer services through Tencent's strengths in big data, AI and cloud computing, Xu said.
Nissan said it and Baidu had signed a memorandum of understanding to carry out research on AI and so-called "smart cars". Nissan will use Baidu's generative AI on its platform to study the feasibility of future tech development, it said.
It will also equip its Chinese cars with Baidu's AI products, it said.
The partnerships also show how competitive China has become for automakers, even globe-spanning giants such as Toyota.
Foreign automakers are fighting to show they can remain relevant in China, amid the pressure from the shift to EVs, the rise of domestic brands and a price war.
Toyota has seen sales shrink, although it has avoided the sharp blows that Honda Motor and Nissan have taken.
It saw its sales in China fall 1.7% to 1.9 million vehicles in 2023, the second successive year of decline.
Toyota also showed off two new battery electric vehicle models for the Chinese market at the Beijing show.

title: The AI camera stripping away privacy in the blink of an eye
text:
It's natural to be leery regarding the ways in which people may use artificial intelligence to cause problems for society in the near future. On a personal level, you may be concerned about a future where artificial intelligence takes your job or creates a Terminator that comes back in time to try to eliminate a younger you. (We admittedly might be overthinking that one.)
One fear regarding AI on a personal level that you should know about because it's very much in the present is the creation of deepfake photos, including those that strip you of the most basic of privacy rights: the right to protect images of your body.
Two German artists recently created a camera called NUCA that uses AI to create deepfake photos of subjects by stripping away their clothing. The automated removal of the photo subject’s clothing occurs in close to real-time, speeding up the creepy factor exponentially.
Why would someone create an AI camera that removes clothing?
The two German artists, Mathias Vef and Benedikt Groß, decided to create the camera to show the implications of AI's rapid advancements. The pair were trying to think of the worst possible uses of AI to affect someone’s privacy, and they realized that the technology needed to create a camera like NUCA was already possible.
WHAT IS ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI)?
The two artists hope that people will consider the dangers of continuing to develop AI technologies like this, which could eliminate the expectation of privacy. They hope it will spark debates about the direction of AI.
MORE: HOW SCAMMERS HAVE SUNK TO A NEW LOW WITH AN AI OBITUARY SCAM TARGETING THE GRIEVING
How does a camera that digitally strips away clothing work?
The German artists used 3D design and print software to create the lenses and the shell for controlling the camera. It then uses a smartphone on the inside of the shell that handles the image capture. NUCA passes the photo to the cloud for the application of AI that removes the subject’s clothing.
Of course, NUCA is not actually creating a photo of your naked body. Instead, it analyzes your gender, face, age and other aspects of your body shape to develop a replication of what AI believes your naked body would look like.

Doesn’t deepfake nude photo technology already exist?
Deepfake nude photos, usually of celebrities, have been around for a long time on pornography websites, but the photos from NUCA require almost no technical know-how.
Even more frightening, NUCA is able to perform the process within about 10 seconds. The immediacy of the creation of the deepfake nude photo is what sets NUCA apart from other fake nude photos that typically require quite a bit of editing skill and time.

NUCA’s deepfake dilemma: Artistic innovation or ethical Invasion?
Bottom line: Anyone could use the technology that’s found with NUCA to create a deepfake nude photo of almost anyone else within several seconds. NUCA doesn’t ask for permission to remove your clothing in the photo.
It's worth emphasizing again that the two artists have no plans to allow others to use NUCA for commercial gain. They will showcase its capabilities in late June at an art exhibition in Berlin all in an effort to spark public debate.
However, the next people who develop a similar technology may choose to use it in a far different way, such as to potentially blackmail people by threatening to release these fake nude photos that other people won’t necessarily know are fake.
Kurt’s key takeaways
If it feels like AI is expanding wildly in dozens of different directions all at once, you aren’t all that far off. Some of those directions will be helpful for society, but others are downright terrifying. As deepfakes continue to look more and more realistic, the line between a fake digital world and reality will become increasingly difficult to discern. Guarding our privacy will almost certainly be more and more difficult as AI strips away our safeguards … and, potentially, even our clothing.

title: Meta shares sink on higher AI spending, light revenue forecast - ET CIO
text:
- Next-Gen Technologies

Meta shares sink on higher AI spending, light revenue forecast
Shares of the Facebook and Instagram parent dropped about 15% in extended trade following the report, its market capitalization plunging to about $1 trillion.
Meta Platforms disappointed investors on Wednesday with forecasts of higher expenses and lighter-than-expected revenue, knocking nearly $200 billion off its stock market value and raising fears the surging cost of AI is outpacing its benefits.
Shares of the Facebook and Instagram parent dropped about 15% in extended trade following the report, its market capitalization plunging to about $1 trillion.
Alphabet shares fell 3% in extended trade and Microsoft declined 2%, with concerns that Wall Street may have underestimated the cost of the AI race hitting those Big Tech companies ahead of their reports on Thursday.
continued below
Meta said it expects April-June revenue in the range of $36.5 billion-$39 billion, with a midpoint of $37.8 billion, compared with analysts' estimates of $38.3 billion, according to LSEG data.
The company raised its forecast for expenses this year to support investments in new AI products and the computing infrastructure needed to support them, adding that it expected spending would continue to increase next year.
It raised its 2024 total expense forecast to $96 billion-$99 billion, from $94 billion-$99 billion. It also expects 2024 capital expenditure to fall within a range of $30 billion-$40 billion, up from its earlier forecast of $35 billion-$37 billion, it said.
CEO Mark Zuckerberg told analysts on a conference call that the focus on AI would "grow our investment envelope meaningfully before we make much revenue from some of these new products."
Zuckerberg's comments and the quarterly results tempered expectations for Meta's AI investments after a series of smash-hit quarters for the social media giant. Meta enjoyed the biggest one-day gain in market capitalization in Wall Street history after its last quarterly report, when it posted robust results and announced a first-ever dividend.
"Investors are skeptical of the growing AI spending. Some of those investments could take years to pay off," said Jasmine Enberg, principal analyst at Insider Intelligence.
"But Meta is in the AI race to win it, and Meta AI could be a dark horse. It has a built-in audience through its existing apps, and it will have an advantage in eventual monetization through its ad ecosystem," Enberg said.
The company has been updating its ad-buying products with AI tools and short video formats to boost revenue growth, while also introducing new AI features like a chat assistant to drive engagement on its social media properties.
It announced last week that it is giving its Meta AI assistant more prominent billing across its suite of apps, meaning it will start to see how popular the product is with users in the second quarter.
"For all Meta's bold AI plans, it can't afford to take its eye off the nucleus of the business - its core advertising activities," said Sophie Lund-Yates, lead equity analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown.
The company's metaverse-oriented Reality Labs division missed expectations for the first quarter, posting sales of $440 million. Investors had been expecting $475 million, according to LSEG data.
The unit's sales leaped 30% from the year prior, but were still below the average revenue of $523 million posted in previous first-quarter reports since Meta started disclosing Reality Labs revenue in 2021.
Reality Labs lost $3.8 billion in the quarter, putting it on track this year to match the $16 billion it lost over the course of 2023.
Zuckerberg also described potential monetization plans for Meta's AI chatbot, such as using it for business messaging and customer support.
Meta theoretically stands to benefit from regulatory pressures bearing down on its Chinese-owned short video competitor TikTok, which is facing the threat of a U.S. ban, although Meta CFO Susan Li told investors she was not yet ready to assess the business impact of the potential setback for its rival.
Meta posted first-quarter revenue of $36.5 billion, roughly in line with expectations of $36.2 billion, according to LSEG data.
Meta's daily active people (DAP), a metric it uses to track unique users of any one of its apps Facebook, Instagram, Messenger or WhatsApp in a day, grew 7%.
DAP grew 8% in the preceding quarter.
Meta disclosed only the DAP figure for user growth, a first for the company. It said earlier this year that it would no longer break out numbers for flagship social network Facebook, whose growth has slowed in recent years.
(Reporting by Yuvraj Malik in Bengaluru and Katie Paul in New YorkAdditional reporting by Noel Randewich in Oakland, California, and Sheila Dang in DallasEditing by Sriraj Kalluvila, Kenneth Li, Matthew Lewis and Tom Hogue)

Britain's competition watchdog said on Wednesday it was seeking comments on the AI partnerships between Microsoft and Mistral AI, as well as between Amazon and Anthropic.
The Competition and Markets Authority also said it wanted to hear the views of third parties on Microsoft's hiring of former employees of Inflection AI and related arrangements.
Microsoft last month appointed DeepMind co-founder Mustafa Suleyman as the head of a newly created consumer AI unit and hired several employees of his Inflection AI startup.
The regulator said it had not formed any conclusions on whether the deals fell within UK merger rules or raised competition concerns.
Microsoft said it was confident that "common business practices such as the hiring of talent or making a fractional investment in an AI start-up promote competition and are not the same as a merger".
"We will provide the UK Competition and Markets Authority with the information it needs to complete its inquiries expeditiously," a spokesperson said.
Amazon said it was "unprecedented for the CMA to review a collaboration of this type".
"Unlike partnerships between other AI startups and large technology companies, our collaboration with Anthropic includes a limited investment, doesn't give Amazon a board director or observer role, and continues to have Anthropic running its models on multiple cloud providers," a spokesperson said.
The CMA is already looking into Microsoft's partnership with Open AI and asked for views in December.
"The CMA is also considering feedback received earlier this year on Microsoft's partnership with OpenAI and is currently waiting for information it has requested from the firms," it said on Wednesday.
